body:
Almost two-thirds of institutional investors expect to increase their exposure to infrastructure equity and private equity over the next three to five years, according to a global survey of 700 investors by IFM Investors.

Infrastructure equity topped the allocation intentions in IFM’s 2026 Private Markets 700 research, with 63% of respondents planning to increase exposure.

Private equity was close behind at 62%, while 55% intend to increase infrastructure debt allocations and 52% expect to add to private debt.

Unlisted real estate was the only private-market category in the survey where fewer than half of respondents planned to increase exposure, at 48%.

The research surveyed institutional investors across 19 countries during May and June, including pension funds, foundations, endowments, insurers, wealth managers and investment consultants.

Of the respondents, 38% were asset owners, 27% insurance companies, 21% wealth managers and 14% consultants.

Infrastructure equity also ranked strongly on expected performance, the report said. Investors targeted average net returns of 10.9% from the strategy, behind the 11.9% expected from private equity but ahead of the 10.4% targeted from unlisted real estate, 10.2% from private debt and 10% from infrastructure debt.

IFM said investors were attracted to infrastructure equity by its exposure to long-term investment themes and potential to provide stable cash flows.

About 44% highlighted exposure to long-term themes as a leading quality of infrastructure equity, while 42% cited stable, long-term cash flows and 39% inflation-linked revenues.

For infrastructure debt, 45% highlighted stable income from contracted assets, 43% its defensive return profile and 40% downside protection.

The research also showed AI and digital infrastructure rising high on investors’ list of sector opportunities.

Advanced technologies including artificial intelligence were identified by 40% of respondents as one of the most attractive areas for private-market investment, ahead of telecommunications and digital infrastructure at 34% and environmental and renewable investments at 30%.

Healthcare and life sciences followed at 26%, with specialty real estate at 23%, conventional energy at 22% and defence and security at 21%.

That enthusiasm is being accompanied by concerns about the volume of capital entering popular investment themes.

IFM found 62% of investors believed inflows into popular themes were putting pressure on prospective returns.

Regional differences were also significant. IFM said 81% of EMEA investors regarded the energy transition as a major long-term opportunity, while 61% of Asian investors excluding Australia showed interest in infrastructure debt.

Australian investors were particularly enthusiastic about infrastructure equity, with 75% expecting to increase allocations.

Liquidity remains an important consideration for those investors. IFM found 68% of Australian respondents said greater liquidity and more flexible redemption terms would encourage additional private-market investment.

The survey found private markets already account for more than a third of respondents’ portfolios.

IFM said the findings showed investors continuing to favour private equity while increasing their interest in infrastructure across both equity and debt strategies.
